chapter: Later career and The Benny Goodman Story
title: CBS staff and the Saturday radio show; leaving for The Benny Goodman Story
summary: He describes the CBS staff job from about 1952 to 1955, the show with Hinton and Jo Jones, and quitting to go to Hollywood for the Goodman film.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: So I was up there about eight years in summer school, and with WNEW about eight, and then I went up to CBS on staff, and I guess that'd be about 1952 or so and I stayed with CBS staff until '55, and of course, at the CBS staff, you know, we had our Saturday afternoon show on the network with you on bass and Jo Jones on drums, and we'd have two guests on each show, and I remember some of the guests were Dizzy, Carmen McRae was a guest at times, and Miss Sarah might have done one or two.

And when we couldn't get a name jazz person that was in town, we would use some of the talented musicians from the staff of CBS, like Artie Drilling er would be on, and sometimes there was another talented alto player
there with us -- it was Pepper something.
Yeah, Pepper. Now what was his last name. [Johnnie Pepper]
Maybe Toots [Monde]lo might have done it.
Because Lou Shoope Shewby sort of suggested who to put on as a guest when we didn't have an outside guest.
And Russ Case was the musical director for that show, wasn't he? He was there in some capacity, I know.

Well, Russ Case was one of the leading conductors they had up there in those days -- Howie Smith, Russ Case, I can hardly remember some of the names, but a lot of musicians were on staff at CBS in those days. Do you remember the Tuesday night -- the show they used to do with Alfredo Antonini, that was a forty-piece band just for radio, all staff musicians at CBS.
It's beautiful to see, when we sit here talking about this, and here is your son, Teddy Wilson Jr. sitting here, and he, and my daughter, used to be running around the studios at the rehearsals.
Right, there's a picture of her right there up there at one of the studios.
Sure. Ted used to come when he was
That's right -- sitting around the studio. Now that show went on -- you stayed on that show until the Benny Goodman story, I think.

Right, uh huh. In 1955 I asked Lou Sherry if I could take leave of absence to work on the Benny Goodman Story for two months, since I had the offer to go out to Hollywood to do that, and Lou Sherry said that, well, this is the early days of TV, so there is no such thing as a two month leave, because in two months, there might not even be any more radio -- because nobody knew what would happen to radio; television was creating such an enormous impact on the industry, and nobody knew just the way things were going to go and how radio could be fitted in with this new phenomenon and had just taken over the entertainment business so much.

So I thought it'd be worthwhile to get back in the public eye, performing on the road, so I quit to do the movie, The Goodman Story, and I'd been out traveling playing from engagement to engagement ever since. After ten years in the studios, I was staying in New York all that time, primarily sticking with the radio and teaching at Juilliard or private teaching.
